To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a single-chip telescope exploiting a single Si chip for both ΔE and E measurements has been tested and that it is a Si-CsI (Tl ) telescope tailored for mass ID of light charged particles (protons, α, Li) and intermediate mass fragments.

(i) the ΔE-E telescope with a single Si chip can be used to identify light charged particles and heavy fragments; (ii) the figure of merit of the telescope with a single chip is similar to that of a conventional telescope with two chips; (iii) the telescope with a Si chip and a CsI(Tl) scintillator can be easily scaled to a large array.

a single-chip telescope can be used for the identification of light charged fragments and intermediate-mass fragments, and the quality of this identification is similar to that obtained by standard ΔE-E telescopes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an efficient, low-cost, and compact telescope for the identification of charged particles.
the development of a single-chip ΔE-E telescope for heavy-ion detection, which can be used in a large solid angle device.
the development of a new type of ΔE-E telescope for heavy-ion detection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present work shows that the single silicon chip configuration can provide a good quality mass identification of light particles and intermediate mass fragment, with a figure of merit that compares favourably to that of standard ΔE-E telescopes.
the presented configuration could be an excellent solution for the front-end of an array of telescopes for heavy ion identification.
the single chip telescope has been shown to be a valid alternative to the traditional ΔE-E telescope.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ΔE-E technique, when applied to the identification of light charged-particle and intermediate mass fragments in a single chip, provides a good compromise between mass resolution and efficiency, while maintaining a simple and inexpensive front-end electronics.
a ΔE-E telescope exploiting only one silicon chip can provide the same identification performance as a ΔE-E telescope with two silicon chips.
the use of a single chip for both ΔE and E detection allows for an excellent identification capability with a very compact and low cost detector.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the single-chip ΔE-E telescope can provide a quality of identification similar to the one of a standard ΔE - E telescope.

a ΔE-E telescope exploiting only one silicon chip can be successfully used for heavy-ion identification in the energy range 20 MeV/nucleon < E < 150 MeV/nucleion, with a performance comparable to that of a conventional two-silicon telescope.
it is possible to identify light charged particles and fragments up to A≈40 in a single silicon chip with a figure of merit comparable to the one obtained with a ΔE-E telescope.
